```{r}
library(tidyverse)
IMDB_movies_data <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/movies_since_2024.csv") |> filter(!is.na(runtimeMinutes), !is.na(averageRating))
```

#Filtering 

I used the filter function you taught us in class with the SoccerFouls activity to filter out any NA inputs found in the runtimeMinutes and averageRating variables. That brought the number of films in the dataset down from 61,834 to 26,829, which is already a much more feasible number to work with.   
# Trial and error testing 

# Runtime summary statistics

```{r}
summary(IMDB_movies_data$runtimeMinutes)
sd(IMDB_movies_data$runtimeMinutes)

```
The mean movie runtime for this dataset is 98.33 minutes. The median runtime is 95, and the standard deviation is 29.22 minutes. These all seem like normal values for movie length. However, I was surprised to see that the minimum movie runtime is 7 minutes, and the maximum is 2,000 minutes. These both seem like pretty extreme values. After looking at the dataset, I discovered that the 7-minute movie is called "Firsts," a short comedy film released in 2025. I didn't account for this dataset to include short films, but I guess it makes sense, and it might be an interesting feature to examine in my larger analysis of the relationship between movie runtime and audience rating. The 2,000 minute movie in this dataset is a 2025 documentary called "The Freedom of Uselessness." Again, I did not think about the fact that documentaries could be included in this dataset. I am not sure if I want to leave documentaries in once I get to testing my hypothesis. Documentaries might be too different from traditional films and therefore might warrant their own separate analysis. 

# Audience rating summary statistics

```{r}
summary(IMDB_movies_data$averageRating)
sd(IMDB_movies_data$averageRating)
```
The mean rating for movies in this dataset is 6.31, the median is 6.4 and the standard deviation is 1.57. The minimum rating is 1. Wow. I had to see which movie this was. Looking at the data, I found it to be "Prazdnik," drama and war movie from 2024. This also a Russian film. I wonder if it is fair to include international films in my analysis, or if it would make more sense to filter them out and narrow down the number of movies I am examining. However, I am unsure how I would do this, since there is no category in the dataset for "langauge" "country" or something similar. Several other movies also received a rating of 1. The maximum rating in this dataset is 10. Again, I was very intrigued to see which movie received such a high rating. I discovered it was the 2025 documentary "I'm Only Blind," along with many others. 

# Scatterplot

```{r}
IMDB_movies_data |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x=runtimeMinutes, y=averageRating)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x=runtimeMinutes, y=averageRating), method="lm")
```

Based on this scatterplot's line of best fit, there seems be a positive relationship between movie runtime and audience rating. However, it is very difficult to tell much about the relationship beyond that, because all of the datapoints are clumped on the left side of the graph, and there are so many of them. I think I need to narrow down the number of movies I include in my analysis based on some parameters. As suggested in the feedback on my last assignment, I think I am going to try filtering out movies that have vote counts below 1,000, and that's just to start. Films with lower vote counts might be less stable and therefore misleading when it comes to my analysis. I am also thinking about excluding movies that run longer than 300 minutes from my analysis, since there are so few of them and they are such outliers. 

# Filter data

```{r}
IMDB_filtered <- IMDB_movies_data |> filter(numVotes >= 1000, runtimeMinutes <= 300)
```

I created a new filtered dataset using the formula we went over in our math scores regression activity in class. I filtered the data so that only films with more than 1,000 vote counts that run less than 300 minutes long are included. This cut the number of movies down from 26,829 to 3,797, a huge difference. Hopefully, it is easier to see trends now.

# Filtered summary statistics

```{r}
summary(IMDB_filtered$runtimeMinutes)
sd(IMDB_filtered$runtimeMinutes)

summary(IMDB_filtered$averageRating)
sd(IMDB_filtered$averageRating)
```
# Filtered scatterplot

```{r}
IMDB_filtered |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x=runtimeMinutes, y=averageRating)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x=runtimeMinutes, y=averageRating), method="lm") +
  labs(x = "Average Rating", y = "Movie Runtime, Minutes",
       title = "Movie Rating vs. Movie Runtime, 2024-26 Films")
```
This is a much clearer scatterplot than before. I can see that there is still a positive relationship between movie runtime and audience rating, but it is very, very slight. There does not seem to be much correlation at all, as all of the datapoints are clumped together in a circle, rather than a clean diagonal line. The slope of the fit line is also very small. 

# Correlation test 

```{r}
IMDB_filtered |> summarize(correlation = cor(averageRating, runtimeMinutes, method="pearson"))
```

This correlation coefficient, 0.24, matches up with what I gathered from the earlier scatterplot. There is a weak positive correlation between movie runtime and audience rating, as 0.24 is much closer to 0, or no correlation, than 1 or -1, or perfect correlation. Based on these findings, I am not confident that I can reject my null hypothesis, which in this case would be that there is no meaningful relationship between movie runtime and audience rating.


# Simple regression analysis

```{r}
movies_model <- lm(averageRating ~ runtimeMinutes, data = IMDB_filtered)
summary(movies_model)
```
The p-value is less than 0.05, which actually means I can reject the null hypothesis after all, because the relationship is statistically significant. Therefore, we can rule out that there is no relationship between movie runtime and audience rating. However, given the correlation coefficient from above, we still know that this relationship is weak. 

The multiple R-squared value is 0.058, meaning that knowing a movie's runtime explains about 5.8% of the variation in expected audience rating. The rest of the variation (most of it in this case) is due to the influence of other factors, potentially things like movie genre, cast, director, etc.

The coefficient value is 0.012. Because this value is positive, it means that as runtimes increase, so movie ratings. However, this value is still extremely small. It tells me that when a movie's runtime increases by 1 minute, its expected audience rating only goes up 0.012%.

# Possible tests

When analyzing this data and testing to see if there is any relationship between movie run time and audience rating, the first thing I would do is look at the descriptive statistics of each relevant variable, in this case "runtimeMinutes" and "averageRating." I would use R's summarize() function to find measurements such as mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum and interquartile range for each variable, similar to how we did for the data in homework 3, White House salaries, and the in-class sleep confidence intervals activity (along with practically every other homework assignment and activity we have been assigned). These kinds of tests would just help me get to know the data better. 

Moving on to analyzing the relationship, or lack thereof, between movie run time and audience rating, I would begin with a null hypothesis test, like the one we did in the hypothesis testing in-class activity a couple of weeks ago. The hypothesis I am interested in testing is that longer movie run times correspond with higher audience ratings, so my null hypothesis would be that there is no meaningful relationship between movie run times and audience ratings. I would use a t-test to see whether or not I can reject the null hypothesis, setting my significance level, or alpha value, to 0.05. If the p-value that comes back from this test is less than 0.05, then I can reject the null hypothesis and confidently say that there is some kind of relationship between movie run time and audience rating. I hope that this is the case, as it would allow me to move forward with the rest of my tests. 

If it does turn out that I can reject the null hypothesis, then I would move on to analyze the correlation between the two variables I am studying. To do this, I would calculate the Pearson's correlation coefficient using the summarize() and cor() functions on "runtimeMinutes" and "averageRating," similar to how we did last class in the soccer fouls and pg murders heat activities as well as over the weekend in homework 15. If the correlation coefficient value is close to + or - 1, that would tell me that movie run times and audience ratings are strongly correlated. If the value is closer to 0, that would mean there is not a very strong relationship between the two variables. Whether the relationship is positive or negative would depend on if the correlation coefficient is above or below 0. A correlation coefficient that would match my hypothesis would be a positive value at least above 0.5, but ideally closer to 1. 

Alongside my correlation test, I would create a scatterplot of movie run times and audience ratings to visually depict the relationship between the two variables. I would use geom_point() and geom_smooth() to do this, just like how we did in our recent assignments. The points on the scatterplot would be arranged in more of a blob/circle if there turns out to be a weak correlation, and a clean, linear, diagonal line if there happens to be stronger correlation. The line of best fit would also be more slanted in the case of strong correlation as opposed to more horizontal in the case of weak correlation. A scatterplot would also allow me to get a more detailed picture of the data and see any outliers in the variable relationship. For instance, if I find that my hypothesis seems plausible and longer movie run times are actually positively correlated with higher audience ratings, there could still be a few contrasting cases, such as a long movie with a low rating or a short movie with a high rating. A few of these outliers would not do much to alter the overall correlation, and therefore could not be indentified without the help of a visual aid like a scatterplot.

Finally, although we haven't actually done any linear regression tests in class yet, after reading about the concept this past weekend, I do think it would make sense for me to do a simple linear regression analysis on movie run times and audience ratings to see how much my dependent variable (audience rating) changes with each increase/decrease in my independent variable (run time). I am sure we will be exploring how to do this in R in class on Wednesday, and I am looking forward to learning how.  

# Data description 

This is a movie and entertainment dataset from the dataset platform Kaggle. According to CourseEra, Kaggle is a platform where data science and machine learning experts can compete and develop models for problem solving. It also provides access to notebooks and skill tutorials. Kaggle offers a wide and diverse range of datasets and machine learning models, all you have to do is search up the topic you are interested in studying and Kaggle will pull up a list of related datasets. That is how I found this movie dataset, because I knew I was interested in doing my final project on entertainment data. https://www.coursera.org/articles/kaggle, https://www.kaggle.com/ 

Moving on to the movie dataset specifically, it includes detailed data for 916 modern feature films from between January 2024 and December 2026. There are 20 total data attributes, all of them individual records, such as movie titles, release dates, genres, audience/critic ratings (out of 10),  vote counts, run times, production budgets, worldwide box office revenue, directors, writers, cast, production studios, content ratings, language, country of origin, plot synopses, and more. Scrolling down, I see that the maker of this dataset collected data from Wikipedia Open API & Public Film Catalogs, Wikipedia OpenSearch API and Unsplash Media, a high-quality film poster website.

As I mentioned above, this dataset contains information on 20 different attributes for each of the 916 films included. The categories range from runtime to audience rating to box office earnings. The time period it covers is January 2024 to December 2026, as it contains some information for movies that have been made but not yet released to the general public. For the sake of my analysis, I plan to take out unreleased movies from this dataset since there might be some misleading or missing data for them. 

The two hypotheses I plan to test are: 
1. Higher production budgets correspond with higher audience ratings.
2. Longer run times correspond with higher audience ratings. 

For this reason, the columns that will be most important to my analysis are "rating_out_of_10," "budget_usd" and "runtime_minutes." Also "title," of course. After examining the data, I can see that there are 29 films coming out in either November or December 2026. Some of them might have come out in the first couple weeks of November, meaning I could include them in my analysis, but I would need to do some deeper digging because there is a lot of missing data for the exact "release_day" category, even for movies that came out in 2024. This is something I might want to keep an eye or on investigate further. I will also actively have to keep track of when upcoming movies are released as we get closer to the due date for our final project. Perhaps to make things easier I will pick a day in the near future when I do my most thorough analysis of the data and use that as my cut off line, even if more movies get released between then and the project due date. I don't want my findings to be constantly changing. 

Professor Willis let me know that budget figures are often missing in movie data, so I took his advice and looked through the dataset for missing budgets. First to rule out any $0 figures, I set the "budget_usd" column so that the lowest numbers came to the top. I found no $0 budgets. Then I scrolled through and looked for any "NA" inputs, also finding none. It looks like all 916 movies included in this dataset have budget data attached to them. However, here is where a whole different problem arose. The lowest value in the dataset is $10,849,306 for the 2025 horror/thriller movie "Ash." Yeah. I immediately became concerned, because that figure seemed way to high for a random movie I had never heard of. Plus, if this was supposed to be the lowest figure in the dataset, that was even more concerning. After a quick Google search, I discovered that Ash's production budget was closer to $500,000. Moving on, the maximum production budget value listed in this dataset is $171,246,357 for the July 2026 movie "Descendants: Wicked Wonderland." First of all, no movie has a budget that high. Second of all, if a movie were to have a budget that high, I can almost guarantee that it would not be in the Descendants franchise. This is data is definitely not accurate, and my findings led me to examine other categories of data more closely. Some of the data does look correct, such as release dates, genres, and names of directors and screenwriters. But the number categories all seem way, way off. Aside from the production budget category, the box office category is also completely false. This dataset claims "Descendants: Wicked Wonderland" earned $510,700,365 at the box office, yet this movie did not even come out in theaters. It debuted on streaming platforms, meaning it had no box office earnings to make. Even the run times aren't really correct.

This is a big bummer, because I was really excited to find this data. I definitely should have taken a deeper look at the data sooner. However, the non-number data in the dataset still seems to be correct, so I could potentially pivot my assignment to explore a different movie-related relationship. For example, I could look at how movie genres and audience ratings correlate. My hypothesis could be that romance movies tend to score higher audience ratings, or alternatively, that sci-fi films tend to score lower audience ratings. 

New IMDB data: https://data.imdb.com/non-commercial-datasets/

```{r}
IMDB_movies_data <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/movies_since_2024.csv")
```

This dataset from IMDB includes 61,834 movies released since 2024 and characteristics such as primary title, original title, genre, run time, average rating and vote numbers. The data here looks accurate -- unlike the first dataset I found -- which is good news because that means I can still explore if there is any relationship between movie run times and average audience ratings for my final project. My hypothesis is that longer movie run times correspond with higher IMDB user ratings. The columns I will study for my analysis are "primaryTitle," "runtimeMinutes" and "averageRating."
